text.en: The Mashgiach reads 'Yehi or' as 'let there be liberty': light is happiness, and the most precious happiness is freedom.
True liberty is not freedom from others' rule but freedom to do the right thing, so a person ruled by his passions is the real prisoner even when he walks about free.
The greatest freedom is to be subservient to no will other than Hashem's.
The Mashgiach describes the future redemption as a repetition of the first Rosh Hashanah, when Hashem's voice will again be heard by all mankind.
The Mashgiach reads the business reason for a trip as mere bait: the true reason a person is brought to a place is a brachah or mitzvah that only he can do there, which he himself does not know.
The rush of summer travel that begins with Tammuz is not by chance: golus is a journey to mend the world, and these months of churban are when the traveling must accomplish the most.

Dan, traveling at the rear and returning lost objects, is a model for the end of every cycle: the end of the year and the end of Jewish history are times of hashavas aveidah, bringing back lost days, mitzvos and souls.
Vayehi binsoa is short because it is unfinished: in the future it will be filled in with every Jew's travels and the mitzvos he did on them, and take its place among the books of the Torah.
Sukkos as the Chag HaAsif is the festival of the lost being gathered back: even Dan, expelled from the clouds of glory, returns under the sukkah of Hashem.
Eretz Yisrael magnifies the neshama: a tzaddik there becomes greater and a rasha more destructive, which the Mashgiach says explains why irreligious people there are more hostile than those abroad.
Some tzaddikim were kept out of Eretz Yisrael not for lack of merit but because their arrival would have brought the Geulah before its time.

The melodious pazer note means scattering: its sweet tune carries the bitter message of the golus, and its seven occurrences in Behaaloscha mirror the seven nations from which the seventy nations of the dispersion branch out.
Seventy is seven multiplied by ten, ten being the number of completeness, so the seventy nations are the seven nations brought to completion.
The seven weeks of nechamah after Tisha b'Av are the counterweight to the seven pazers, and the comfort is that the golus was good all along, as will become clear when Moshiach comes.
Adding a name to a gravely sick person works when his illness comes because he has finished his shlichus: the new name is a new shlichus and an addition to his neshamah.
The summer vacation season falls in Tammuz, when the spies set out, so that the travels of Jews today can repair the spies' failed shlichus and bring the geulah.
The Nefilim whom the spies saw were angels who fell from their level, and their name was a hint to the spies not to fall; the spies missed it.
The cantillation note 'pazer' (scatter) appears seven times in Beha'aloscha, read just after Chof Sivan, mirroring in reverse the seven weeks of Sefirah that gathered Klal Yisrael to Shavuos.
A traveler's own reason for a trip is not Hashem's reason: the businessman goes to Chicago for a meeting, but Heaven sends him for one glass of water that needs his brachah.
Even the work of a gentile is for a Jew: the miner who produces steel is related in some way to the Jew who stirs his coffee with a spoon made from it.
Changing a sick person's name works because a name is a shlichus: if he is departing because his mission is done, a new name gives him a new mission to live for.
The summer 'travel fever' of Tammuz and Av is a soul's urge to repair the meraglim's failed journey in the same season.
Tammuz and Av belong to Reuven and Shimon, the shevatim whose nesi'im failed, which is why these two months fell, though by right Reuven and Shimon should have been first.
Yehoshua and Kalev, who did not join the meraglim, came from Ephraim and Yehuda, the shevatim of Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben David, so the faithful shluchim are tied to the geulah.

The Mashgiach reverses the Chasam Sofer's order: the people asked first, and Hashem added Himself as a sender so His intention would also count, giving the meraglim a choice; that is why Kalev and Yehoshua were saved.
The angel's 'why do you ask my name' was not evasion but his real name: the mission of the yetzer hara is to make a person refuse to ask about his own name and mission.

In 'yemei bikurei anavim', 'bikurei' hints to the letters that come before those of 'anavim', which spell the names of the Satan, and the full spelling of 'Amalek' equals the gematria of 'yemei bikurei anavim'.
By reason the meraglim were right that Klal Yisrael could not conquer the land; their sin was relying on their understanding where Hashem had said they could, instead of going with emunah.

Tzitzis hang at the bottom edge of the garment just as this generation stands at the end of history; Klal Yisrael has been weaving one garment since Matan Torah, and the last thread, where tzitzis go, is where Moshiach is found.
Krias Shema's last word, 'emes', is not written in the parsha and must be added and called out, a sign that in the end of days the truth is hidden and has to be dug out.
Shlichus requires a neshama that is a part of G-d; a non-Jew cannot be a shaliach, and the concept was first given with the korban Pesach when the Jews became a people.

Pharaoh knew the righteous midwives would never kill, so he first stripped them of their Jewish names: the name itself is a dike of kedushah, and once it is breached by a name of tumah the rest can follow.
The 'al tikri' of shamos as shemos is not a change of reading: the devastations that astound people can only be understood through the names, the missions, of those who suffer them.
The Gemara's question where Moshe is hinted in the Torah asks who Moshe was before he was born; the answer is Noach, and the teivah and rescue from water repeat in Moshe's life.
Moshe's 'mecheini' is a rearrangement of 'mei Noach': by risking himself for his generation he repaired Noach's failure to daven for his.
Bereishis teaches visible reward and punishment, while Shemos opens with unexplained suffering and immediately lists names, telling that the sufferers had missions.

Just as the same letters of Hashem's name give Nissan or Teves depending on their order, two people with the same name may have different inner arrangements; free choice decides tzaddik or rasha, not one's traits.
The final letters of 'Bnei Yisrael haba'im Mitzraymah' spell milah: the names in Shemos are given like names at a bris, on the day of geulah.
The Mashgiach links the 600,000 Shabbosos of the world's history to the 600,000 souls of Israel and the 600,000 letters of the Torah: just as every soul is unique, no Shabbos ever repeats.
What the sedra describes happens again spiritually that week: on Shabbos Vayera Hashem visits a sick generation as He visited Avraham on the third day after his milah.
Because both Rosh Hashanah readings are in Vayera, this Shabbos carries something of Rosh Hashanah, and one who feels his Rosh Hashanah was lacking can complete it then.
The proof of Avraham's simcha is that he walked at the same pace as Yitzchak, who did not know, and that he returned 'together' as if he had done nothing special.
Yitzchak's milah at eight days was not a loss of a chance for devotion: it shows that a Jew is a Jew by birth, beyond choice, while Yishmael's devotion is only a matter of the mind, like tefillin.
The Rambam's explanation of coerced consent shows that a Jew's true will is always to do Hashem's will; the flogging only subdues the body from which the yetzer hara comes.
Mesiras nefesh of whole communities without exception is explained by intrinsic love, which needs no reason, as opposed to devotion that must be trained and indoctrinated.
The Mashgiach reads the Gemara's 100 versus 101 times as a definition: being an oved Hashem is measured by going beyond one's own accepted standard, not by the level one has reached.
A masmid who fought his way to eight hours of learning a day was an oved Hashem while he struggled, but once that is his routine and he stops striving he is 'lo avado' again.

The Mashgiach links Beis Hillel's adding a candle to 'do good' and Beis Shammai's decreasing to 'turn from evil', and shows that the mehadrin's growth applies to holding back from sin as well, such as taking on stringencies in kashrus.

Building on the Chasam Sofer's reading of Chashmonaim as 'oil' and 'eight', the Mashgiach reads the letters of Chanukah as 'kohen' and eight: for eight days every Jew is a kohen preparing the lights in his home, which becomes like a Mikdash.
The Mashgiach explains the Rambam's calling Chanukah especially cherished through Rashi's reason that milah was dear to Avraham Avinu: what comes through pain and mesiras nefesh becomes beloved.

The unprecedented temptations of modern times, from new inventions to the state of the streets, are the Satan's 'last meal' before he is slaughtered, granted so that it will be tested who serves Hashem.
Since nefesh means one's will, holding back from a desire, such as a clever joke at someone's expense or a word during seder, is real mesiras nefesh, a small fraction of the Akeidah.

Nitzavim with its 40 pesukim comes before Vayeilech with 30, although Rosh Hashanah precedes Yom Kippur, because the Torah follows the majority, who are not tzaddikim gemurim and need the full 40 days.
The 122 pesukim of Ki Savo look back: they reproach the 122 days of teshuvah that were given last year and not used, which is why the year ended with curses.

The Torah states 30, 40 and 52 days openly, but the full 122 only through a combination of three sedros, because it is shameful to need until Chanukah, just as Moshe's rebuke was given by hint out of respect for Klal Yisrael.

The 48th and 50th pesukim of Haazinu, matching the fourth and sixth days of Sukkos, name Moshe and Aharon openly and hint at Yosef in both, so that the Chassidic and Ashkenazic orders of the ushpizin each have a source and neither is slighted.
Even a first thought of the Gemara that it later abandons is Torah: deriving the sukkah's height from the kapores reveals a real bond between the sukkah and the Kodesh HaKodashim.

Sukkah and Chanukah are opposites: the sukkah stays above ten tefachim like the Shechinah, while the Chanukah light is placed below ten, on the left side, in the public domain and the long nights of Teves, bringing holiness into the realm of darkness.
Years of pekidah have often been tragic precisely because they are fitting for Moshiach: the Satan, knowing Moshiach means his end, brings up the sins of Klal Yisrael to accuse them.

The number of pesukim in Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu mirrors the stages of judgment: 40 for those who need Elul and the Aseres Yemei Teshuvah, 30 for tzaddikim, 52 until Shemini Atzeres, and 122 together until Zos Chanukah.
Ki Savo's own 122 pesukim belong to the outgoing year: they point an accusing finger at the 122 days of teshuvah that were granted last year and not used.
Zos Chanukah is a concentrate of all 122 days, so on it a person can run through the whole period again and do teshuvah.

The Ba'al HaTurim's link between Yishmael's falling at the end of Chayei Sarah and 'Yitzchak ben Avraham' right after teaches that Moshiach, from Yitzchak, comes when Yishmael falls suddenly at his height.
Among the seven barren mothers, the seventh is Tziyon; so the Rosh Hashanah kriah of Sarah's remembrance is really a tefillah for Yerushalayim's children to return.
The second part of the Rosh Hashanah kriah, Sarah's demand to send away Yishmael because the land belongs to Yitzchak, is the tefillah to be saved from the fear of Yishmael.
Kinah is the first flaw in creation itself: before any human sin, the moon's envy of the sun caused it to be diminished.

The Mashgiach stresses that Kayin's murder is no newspaper item about ordinary people: Kayin was a great man, a son of Adam, to whom Hashem spoke, and this shows how far kinah can drag even a great person.
According to the Midrash Kayin's 'Am I my brother's keeper?' is a complaint against Hashem, the Keeper of the world, for not holding him back and for giving him such jealousy.
The Berditchever turned the blood libel around: the 'blood' that must not go into matzos is the suffering of the widows rushed in the bakery.
Heaven judges the shame caused to another even when the act was permitted: Reb Mordechai Banet was right al pi halachah to end the shidduch, yet he was penalized for shaming the kallah.
The Mashgiach notes that the young ilui is held responsible even though at seventeen he had not yet had time to work on his middos.

Although the soul is the holy part, the Mashgiach says a person came into the world for the sake of the body: the soul came down only to purify the animal-like body until the body itself can share in dveikus.
The Mashgiach reads tefillah and tefillin as one root meaning to attach; tefillin must be bound tight, and tefillah is the same tight binding of the heart to Hashem.
Even a prayer for one's own needs, which is not for its own sake, is itself a fulfillment of emunah, because one asks only Him whom one believes can give.
Asking Hashem for a small thing is a small request but great emunah, since one recognizes that every great and small thing comes only from Him.

The Mashgiach shows from the Mishnah of one who sets his Shabbos boundary at a distant tree that a person is legally where his thought is, which explains how one davening far away is in the Beis HaMikdash.
In the poritz story, the Mashgiach notes with irony that the poritz would never find his mistake because he does not say Shemoneh Esrei, the time when some Jews do their accounts.
The Mashgiach reads the Mishnah's 'I made its damage possible' as saying that a person's property is an extension of his nefesh, so the owner of a damaging ox is himself the source of the damage.

He reads the categories of damage as the owner's middos showing through his animal: goring reflects a will to harm, eating another's grain reflects desire, and trampling reflects carelessness about others.
Because a friend is part of one's nefesh, a person who becomes a true baal middos will make his friends into baalei middos too.

The four levels of Torah correspond to the levels of the soul, so the Zohar's stringencies and Rav's ruling for Rabbah bar bar Chana are the halachah for a person on a higher level, not a departure from it.
From the Akeidah, where Hashem Himself commanded the slaughter but an angel sufficed to stop it, Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin learned that a command to harm a Jew is not accepted even from a great angel.
The Mashgiach connects Rabbi Chaim of Volozhin's refusal to harm a Jew with the unbroken chain of great descendants he merited, unusual among the Litvish.
Rabbi Yonasan Eybeschutz, the great posek of Choshen Mishpat, saw his long davening, not his learning, as his portion from all his toil, because davening is dveykus.
The closed window of Bilgah mirrors a closed heart: what exists in Heaven exists in man, so a heart closed to the avodah closes the source of blessing above.

The camp of Israel in the desert is also a camp in time: the generation of the giving of the Torah is the front and the generation of Moshiach is Dan, the rear guard, whose flaw of lateness it must repair.
The very difficulty a person meets in a mitzvah he longs for is the sign that it is the mitzvah he came into the world for, since the yetzer hara blocks it most.
Amalek 'cooled' Israel on the way; a Jew's heart must burn with warmth and zerizus, and coldness is what makes a person slow.
A soul that was zariz in Torah and mitzvos in life arrives on time for its tikkun after life, while one that was late in life comes late then too.
A person's life is itself his song to Hashem, so killing is cutting off another Jew's song in the middle.
The killer is like the sun at Givon: because he stopped another's song, his own song falls silent and his life force is diminished.
The Levi'im heal the killer the way a tuning fork sets off a matching piano string: their song is tuned to every Jewish soul and awakens it.
David's harp played by itself at midnight because his soul was tuned to the same note as the song of Gan Eden at chatzos.
Since every sin holds something of killing, Shabbos serves as a city of refuge for every Jew, and Kabbalas Shabbos completes the seven voices.
The Mashgiach reads the parable of the snake and the king's daughter as the struggle with the yetzer hara whose prize is genuine tefillah.
The unprecedented strength of today's tests is itself a sign of how great the reward will be.
The Mashgiach links the new tests of this generation with a new form of Torah, its inner dimension, being revealed.
The weeks of consolation are a progression through the middos, so each week's consolation has its own character: chessed, then yirah.
Yiras Shamayim itself is presented as a consolation, not a burden.
The word Bereishis holds the letters of 'yarei Shabbos', showing that Shabbos gives yiras Shamayim.
There is a special joy in fear of sin, and this is the avodah of the parsha.
Even the Communist commissar recognized the Rebbe's total self-giving for others, and described it in his own terms as being a true 'communist'.
The Sekulener Rebbe weighed his own danger against the other Jew's life and judged that he must go, with mesirus nefesh.
His joy at the end came from the Jew's release, not from his own safety: he had been thrown down the stairs.
The Mashgiach presents being confined in Yerushalayim as something Jews prayed for their whole lives.
If confinement must come, the Mashgiach suggests, at least let it be in Yerushalayim.
He brings the example of a great chassid who was confined in Yerushalayim, showing that such confinement befitted even great people.
The name Kinneres hints at the kinor: the seventh sea completes the set as the seventh note completes the scale, and the lake is even shaped like a violin.

The passuk's border that 'touches the shoulder of Yam Kinneres' is read as the Shechinah going around Eretz Yisrael on Shabbos and giving the singing Kinneres an approving pat on the shoulder, like the Stoliner's pat to the Blazhever Rav.
No person has the strength to sing before the Ribono shel Olam on his own; it is only because Shabbos itself sings that Jews can join in.
The secret of a niggun is the unity of its notes, each joined to the next, which is why song fits Shabbos, the day of 'echad'.
A Shabbos meal that lacks divrei Torah and holiness is like a feast prepared for a king who was never invited: Shabbos, the queen, must be called in.
Healing comes from tiferes and hod, the middos of harmony and balance, which is why a mi sheberach for the sick is said after the fifth aliyah, and illness is an imbalance in the body.
Musical harmony is three notes apart because the third middah is tiferes, and the chord adds the fifth, hod: the laws of music follow the middos.
The half-tones are the middah of din, since halving is division; a tune only on the black keys comes out sad, yet broken notes like shevarim and teruah also blend into the great song.
The blank spaces in Shiras HaYam are as much part of the song as the letters, just as the empty periods of a person's life belong to his song to Hashem.
Singing a niggun an octave lower when one cannot reach the high notes keeps the same tune, and this is the way of teshuvah: going down to rise to the eighth.
The rasha also has a shirah, his own downfall, which is why Esav's angel fought Yaakov exactly when his time to sing arrived.
The Kinneres is the seventh sea and the harp of the world, and every Jew, a small world, has his own Kinneres; a Jew who does not sing on Shabbos is as if his seas dried up.

The Mashgiach explains that the pleasure of a song or niggun is not in any word or note but in the connection between them, and this is what David meant by calling the Torah zemiros: its smuchim are its music.
The seven days of creation are seven notes of an octave; only with the seventh note, Shabbos, can music be played, which is why Shabbos alone has a 'mizmor shir' and why the Torah has seven books.

The four blank lines between the books, from which a get's twelve lines are learned, mirror the exile as a divorce; in the future they will be revealed as the white of the Torah sheb'al peh, showing there never was a get.

David, the soul of Moshiach, lived in the future state in which the whole Torah is song; he was right, but was punished for saying it before its time, and so the Rambam rules according to the present.
Sefer Devarim, whose four lines are not counted for the get, is the seventh book, the book of song and of Moshiach, and it begins on Shabbos Chazon, the day before Tisha b'Av, when Moshiach is born.
The Kinneres, named for the kinor, is the shaliach tzibbur of the seas, completing the seven like Shabbos among days and Eretz Yisrael among lands.

The summer travel season falls exactly on the spies' forty days, from erev Rosh Chodesh Tammuz to Tisha b'Av; Hashem sends Jews travelling then so that by travelling as true shluchim they rectify the spies' journey.
The spies' sin was that while touring the land they forgot they were shluchim and saw only what they wanted; this is the danger of every trip.
A tree in the Catskills has waited thousands of years for a particular boy to make a bracha with kavanah on its apple; only then is it raised up and fulfils the purpose for which it was created.
When a Jew davens in the morning he calls on all creation, the mountains, trees, animals and birds, to praise Hashem with him, and the mitzvos he does in a place are their mitzvos too.
In the parable's lesson, worldly treats are the tallow candles: prized down here, but spoiled and thrown away at the gate of the next world, where only Torah and mitzvos, the diamonds, are let in.

In the city Hashem's creation is hidden behind buildings, so one sees only what people made; the country reveals His heavens, fields and creatures, and this is a chance to reach love and fear of Hashem.
A name is like a battery: it does not only describe a person's mission but supplies the strength to carry it out, which is why a sick person may be given an added name with a new mission.

Pharaoh's two separate commands to the midwives were a strategy: Egyptian names would draw tumah onto them, after which they would obey an order to kill; their refusal to take the names was what saved the children.

The Gemara's 'do not read shamos but shemos' answers the question of bewildering destruction: such a generation is not mere ruin but a gathering of souls with a shared mission to repair a flaw in creation.
Even the English word 'calling' reflects that a mission and a name are one: what a person is called is what he is called to do.
'Shem' (name) shares a root with 'sham' (there) and 'shamayim': a name belongs to the remote, heavenly realm, which is why the reasons behind names and missions are beyond human grasp.
Chazal read Hagar's 'vateta' as a return to idolatry because a believer cannot be physically lost; the only real straying is from Hashem.
The obstacles that keep blocking a person's strong desire are a sign that this is his mission, since that is where the Satan fights hardest.

Malki-Tzedek's blessing of Avraham before Hashem, for which he lost the kehunah, is read by the Mashgiach as also an acknowledgment that Avraham was greater, through whom he could reach a higher bittul to Hashem.
Yerushalayim is the Shabbos of the world: like Shabbos, it produces nothing of its own, and for that very reason it is the source of blessing.
The miracle that the people stood crowded yet bowed with room is explained by bittul: one who is batel to Hashem takes up no space.

A king of Dovid's house may sit in the Azarah because his complete bittul makes him part of the building itself, like its stones and wood; this also explains why Dovid is mentioned right before the closing of Boneh Yerushalayim.
In Avraham's war with the kings, throwing dust was not a lack of trust but an expression of bittul: before Hashem the kings were nothing, like dust.
The law that the avodah is done standing appears among the people's duties to the kohen because the kohen's standing bittul is the very reason one is batel to him.

The kohen's duty to stand during the avodah is not a law of the avodah but of mora Mikdash and bittul, which is why the Torah places it among the 'rights of the kohanim' in Shoftim rather than in Vayikra.

Malki Tzedek's loss of the kehunah was not a punishment but a revelation of the truth: ordinary people must begin by accepting a rebbe, while the king of Yerushalayim, the highest, had to begin with praise of Hashem Himself.

There is no aliyah l'regel on Rosh Hashanah and Yom Kippur because then the King comes to every Jew; on the festivals the Jew goes to the King, but on the Yamim Noraim His kingship spreads over the whole world.

Kings of the house of David may sit in the Azarah because David's bittul made him like the dust of the Azarah, part of the building of the Mikdash, just as earth placed in a sukkah becomes part of it only when wholly batel.

The 'giving' of the weekdays to Shabbos, of the world to Yerushalayim and of the unlearned to the talmid chacham is like the people giving to their king: in truth it is the receiver who sustains the giver.
Eretz Yisroel is Rosh Hashanah in place, Rosh Hashanah is Eretz Yisroel in time, and the tzaddikim are it in soul; this is why chassidim traveled to their rebbe for Rosh Hashanah.

Aharon's garments and Achashverosh's display share the same word, 'tiferes', but the Kohen Gadol wore that beauty for Hashem's honor, while Achashverosh used it 'to show', and that difference separates holy beauty from luxury.

Achashverosh was not punished for wearing the priestly garments, which are royal garments worn by a king, but at once for giving the holy vessels to common guests, because that debased malchus itself.
Achashverosh made the hidden frames of his beds silver and the visible legs gold, the opposite of the Ruzhiner tzaddik's rule that what one lacks inside one does not show outside.
Shmuel HaRamasi took his vessels with him because 'his home was in Ramah': his home was on high, so here, on his journey, he needed nothing, just as the Chofetz Chaim answered his visitor.
The Samael flees to Botzrah because 'botzrah' means strength: he flees to his strength, the female side, which is why the end of galus brings a rise of the feminine side of the sitra achra.
The verse says Vashti made a 'women's feast', not a feast 'for women', because it was a feast with a cause: a convention to raise the standing of women, like the movements of the Mashgiach's day.
Both readings of Memuchan, Haman and Daniel, are true: Haman was Daniel's bad side, and Daniel's prayers for the rebuilding were carried out through Haman's advice to remove Vashti.
The Mashgiach reads the order of the parshiyos as a lesson: Shemini, right after Pesach, guards what enters the mouth, and Tazria-Metzora then guards what leaves it.
Since today the tefillos stand in place of the korbanos, the mouth is the mizbeach, and food that is not truly kosher defiles the altar on which the tefillah is offered.

The great tzaddikim of earlier generations already built the large parts of the heavenly Beis HaMikdash; the generation's task is only the finishing touches, and the King of Glory will not enter until they are done.

A test is measured by the person: refusing a doubtful candy or holding back a joke would be laughable as a test for the Chofetz Chaim, yet for a child it is a real nisayon, and so it counts in building the Beis HaMikdash.
The metzora's covered mouth is the fitting response to a mouth that was not bound when he was healthy; a Jew's mouth is not hefker.
Restraint known to no one but Hashem is exactly what goes up to heaven and polishes the Beis HaMikdash.

The Mashgiach reads the signs of Moshiach like weather: heavy clouds with thunder and lightning make rain likely but not certain, and so the world's present turmoil makes the redemption very near without promising it.
A bachur's zeal in coming on time to davening and seder is, measure for measure, an awakening above that the redemption should come early and not be postponed.
For a bachur without money, tzedakah can be giving time to a downcast friend, encouraging him and cheering him up, and this too hastens Moshiach.
The Sanzer Rav's remark on the rotten bekeshe teaches that a garment of mitzvos done with excuses looks whole but tears at every touch in the next world.
Immersing in the morning in honor of Moshiach's coming, as one immerses in honor of Shabbos to receive its light in purity, is a way of fulfilling the mitzvah of hoping for the redemption.

Because all Jews are bound together, a small act of purity such as washing negel vasser purifies not only the person but his friends, Klal Yisroel and the whole creation, the reverse of how the generation of the Flood corrupted it.
The meraglim lacked Moshe Rabbeinu's power because, as Devarim shows, the people asked for the mission, so the spies were really the agents of a people that included men with flawed intentions.

The travel that begins in Tammuz and Av, the months of the meraglim's journey, is arranged by Hashem as a repair of their failed mission, and had Jews traveled with this awareness Moshiach might already have come.
The angel's seemingly disrespectful 'why do you ask my name' was not sarcasm but his mission speaking: the yetzer hara's task is to make people stop asking what their mission is.

The word emes, which closes Shema but is not written in the Torah's parsha, reflects the generation of the heels before Moshiach, when truth is absent; precisely because it is hidden it must be cried out.
The sin of the meraglim was politics: as nesiim they knew that entering Eretz Yisroel would bring new leaders, and the generation before Moshiach faces the same test of partisan disputes.
A tzaddik read 'yoshvei kranos' as those who sit in the beis medrash with horns, learning but goring others so they feel unwelcome.
The two parshiyos written out of place, Pesach Sheni and Vayehi binsoa, are themselves the 'letters' of souls in exile, and their displacement in the Torah is their tikkun.
Clothing is a garment of malchus shamayim, so stripping down in the country is the very symbol of throwing off the yoke of Heaven.

The order of the camps' travel maps onto the months: Gershon and Merari are the exiled souls, Reuven and Shimon, unblessed by Yaakov, are Tamuz and Av, and Gad, Eliyahu's tribe, brings the consolation.
Inserting a yud into the spies' 'anavim' removes the Satan's name hidden in it, which is the work of a Jew who brings holiness into Tamuz and Av.
The spies' grapes, the instrument of their sin, became wine for the nesachim, showing that the days of their failure are meant to become the tikkun.
Tefillah was the one thing that separated Kalev and Yehoshua from the other spies, so the defense in these days is to pray not to stumble.
The Mashgiach reads Chazal's parting wish that no talmid 'spoil his dish in public' as a call to every ben Torah to guard against chillul Hashem when he goes out among strangers.
He explains Devorah's name as a bee, which goes around buzzing 'bin, bin' ('I am, I am'), a picture of one who thinks himself great.
Group pride, whether nation, team, chassidus or beis medrash, is one kelipah with many names, and a bachur should not display it among others.
Since the Beis Hamikdash is almost complete, what is missing today is like a thumbtack, and holding back a cutting joke or a look in the street supplies it.
Chizuk is like vitamin C, which the body does not store, so yesterday's chizuk is gone and must be taken again today.
A bachur who has no money to give maaser can give maaser of his time to help another.
The summer camp season, which falls in the days the meraglim went out, is a chance to repair their failed mission by being faithful shluchim.
Korach's dispute was split within itself because each side sought itself; only when all seek Hashem's honor are they bound together, even in disagreement.
The Mishnah ends one perek with 'all needs of milah are done on Shabbos' and opens the next by continuing it, to teach that hilchos milah are themselves hilchos Shabbos.
Avraham delayed his milah so it could fall on Yom Kippur, the root of Shabbos, because milah must be bound up with Shabbos.
A loud voice in tefillah is not for Hashem to hear but to awaken the one davening; this answers the Pri Megadim's question.
Iyov was punished for his silence even though shouting would not have helped, because one who truly feels the pain cries out regardless.
The Rosh Chodesh meal is the Jews' share in the korban Hashem asked for the diminished moon: like kohanim eating a korban, their seudah is a pleasing offering before Hashem.
Shaul's fury at Dovid's family feast came because the seudah of Rosh Chodesh belongs to the king; a Rosh Chodesh feast of Dovid looked to him like rebellion, a seudah of Moshiach.

The Yismach Moshe, who could eat soap water without noticing, does not refute the rule that man needs pleasure; he proves it, since no one enjoyed the world more than he did through Gemara and tefillah.
Hashem can forgive a person for the taavos he was created with, but one who brings in new ones has gone far beyond them, to the other side of the sea.
Even overindulging in a Jewish piece of kugel is kelipas nogah that can be elevated, but goyish pleasures cannot be, and that is the meaning of 'do not rejoice like the nations'.
Gan Eden and Gehinnom are one place: the same long davening is Gan Eden for one who is connected to it and Gehinnom for one who is not.
The seudah of Rosh Chodesh is itself a miracle like the survival of avodas Hashem: the moon that died rises again, like techiyas hameisim, and it is the meal of Dovid, king of Israel, who lives on.
The Mashgiach reads the threats and hardships of his own day, Iran and the economic crisis, as the same kind of 'history-making' darkness that came just before the Exodus and the Purim miracle.
Since Iran is the ancient Paras where Haman fell, and a place where Jews had a miracle, the Mashgiach hopes for a repeat of that same miracle there in his day.
The lack of money to give is compared to Pharaoh's decree of bricks without straw: Hashem deliberately leaves the givers with only a little, so that giving becomes mesiras nefesh.

Tamar's indirect hint to Yehuda, rather than open disclosure, was a plan so that both of them would act with mesiras nefesh, the only thing that could defeat the Satan's efforts against the birth of Moshiach's line.
Hashem's 'gift' to Lot, by which he was saved, was guests whom he had to take in with mesiras nefesh; in the same way the needy kallahs of today are Hashem's present to those who can help.
From 'im yesh es nafshechem' the Mashgiach learns that nefesh means will, so mesiras nefesh is acting against one's own will for Hashem, not only giving up one's life.
The 101st review is what makes an oved Hashem because it goes past the routine of a hundred and takes mesiras nefesh.

The Mashgiach presents the dispute between the Ba'al HaTanya and the other students of the Maggid not as a question of truth, since both views are true, but of which path to teach the masses: the Ba'al HaTanya demanded that ordinary people learn chochmah of G-dliness, while the others may have done so themselves but worked differently with the public.
He likens this to the dispute between Yosef and his brothers: whether to work with a few strong, great people in a concentrated way or with many, where each receives only a little.

The same divide, he says, separated the Ba'al HaTanya from Rabbi Mottel of Chernobyl: whether the Rebbe lifts up the chassidim, who bind themselves to him, or whether the chassidim must lift themselves.

The Mashgiach finds the Tanya's path in the order of the brachos of Krias Shema: Yotzer contemplates the luminaries and the angels and brings fear, Ahavah Rabbah brings love, and only then come Shema and Vehaya, accepting the yoke of Heaven and of the mitzvos.

Shechem's intense words of desire for Dinah came from a hidden spark of Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon within him that longed for its own kind; from this the Mashgiach learns that a Jew, a part of G-d above, must long for Hashem in the same way.
He adds that the love-language came specifically through Shechem because Rabbi Chanina ben Teradyon was a devoted gabbai tzedakah, a spark of chesed, and chesed is love.

The Mashgiach explains the Satmar Rav's answer, that korbanos could be taken from Egyptian animals because on the night of Yetzias Mitzrayim all the idolatry was utterly destroyed, as a sample of the end of days, when evil will be nullified at its root.

A person who cannot yet long for Hashem should at least long to long, a will to have a will; when it comes from the depth of the heart, it draws a light of the future and can uproot even the three impure kelipos already in galus.
The present wave of teshuvah is like the drizzle that comes before a long, heavy rain: a sign that the great teshuvah of the days of Moshiach is near.

The Gemara's 'one of us is like two of them' is seen plainly in that nearly all the leading rabbanim and roshei yeshivah of Eretz Yisrael came from abroad, because one who tears himself out of galus arrives with a greater thirst.

Since the sin is what made him a ba'al teshuvah, it becomes part of his greatness; for the same reason, one who sins planning to repent cannot elevate the sin, because there the teshuvah caused the sin.

The Torah writes wasted seed only by hint and not as an explicit prohibition precisely because it is easier to repair: since the Torah is truth, an explicit lav would leave no room for the tzaddikim's advice for its tikkun.
The view that nothing is truly 'reshus' and everything is either a mitzvah or a sin fits the Tanya: the thing itself stands on the scale, and only what one does with it decides.
The Creator made a composition and wrote a commentary on it: the world is the composition and the Torah is its commentary, so only one who learns Torah understands what the world is.
The wells Avraham and Yitzchak dug are the search for the 'well of living water', the point of G-dliness inside earthly things, and Yitzchak dug them as a path for all of Klal Yisroel in exile.
The Torah can tell at length of Yaakov tending Lavan's sheep, which no biographer would write of a great man, because one who learns with emunah knows these were not plain dealings.
Yitzchak blessed Yaakov with material bounty rather than Torah because the strength of the Avos was to enter material things and raise the holy sparks hidden in them.
The Torah cannot set how much a person should eat, because what is for Heaven's sake for one is too much for another; it can only forbid treif.
Even when the food itself rises through later Torah and tefillah, the imprint of the pleasure taken not for Heaven remains, and this is what chibut hakever removes.

Teshuvah out of love is a private arrival of Moshiach: just as in the days of Moshiach the sitra achra will be nullified, so in the small world of the one who returns out of love it is already nullified, which is why he can repair what for the world at large waits for Moshiach.
Since Hashem is reshus hayachid and the klipah is reshus harabim, hotza'ah is the heart of Shabbos, and Gehinnom and machlokes were created on the second day, when plurality began.
Kislev opens with Yaakov leaving Eretz Yisrael for reshus harabim, and the avodah of Chanukah is to light a candle in reshus harabim, making Har Eisav into Har Tziyon.
Chanukah's eight days come from Binah, eight levels above Malchus, and teshuvah out of love is Binah; so teshuvah out of love lifts a Jew to the very place Chanukah comes from.
A mamzer cannot be repaired in a moment because the klipah has dug itself into time through a nine-month process, so only sustained teshuvah can spread into the mamzer's body and cut off its life.

Halachic rulings follow Providence: the Mishnah Berurah's ruling that food eaten unknowingly or under coercion can be elevated was placed in his heart so that the cantonist children would not be left with a sealed heart unable to return.
The Tzemach Tzedek reads the Tanya through the laws of bracha acharonah: a bracha elevates the sparks in the food, so where no bracha may be said, the food has no elevation.

The chapter sits at the border between weekday and Shabbos because its eighteen Names correspond to the weekday Shemoneh Esrei and its seven voices to the Shabbos Amidah, so it carries the holy letters and Names needed to draw down the Shabbos soul.

Kabbalas Shabbos is done with this chapter because its theme, bitul, is malchus, and Shabbos, the day Hashem rejoices in His completed creation, is when a person proclaims he is Hashem's creature and nullifies himself to His kingship.
Shabbos is the day of bitul because on it a Jew does no work and produces nothing; he is simply nothing before Hashem.
Yosef's greatest bitul was joining his brothers' minyan for the oath, letting himself be counted in the very decision to sell him.
A tzaddik who praises himself may be fully humble, since he credits the gift to Hashem and is really praising Hashem, as David says 'baHashem tishallel nafshi'.
The voice of Hashem that one hears in the world's beauty is the same voice in its destruction and upheavals; both are part of one harmony.
Simcha and safek are opposites: doubt is insecurity, simcha is security, so Amalek, whose gematria is safek, attacks joy by attacking faith.

Amalek 'karcha baderech' means he made everything into mikreh, chance; the word mikreh in this sense does not belong in a Jew's vocabulary and is the voice of the forces of impurity that hide Hashem's face.
The 'heel' generations at the end of exile parallel Adar, the last and lowest month, which is why Amalek thought he could prevail over the Jews in it.
The written 'lo' with an alef and the read 'lo' with a vav in 'v'lo anachnu' contrast how things look in the newspapers, 'we are not His people', with the truth of the Oral Torah, 'we are His'.
The Samech-Mem rules up to one hundred, so the hundred brachos with amen, like learning a hundred and one times, carry a person beyond its domain.
Thanks (todah) is the gate and tehillah is the inner courtyard: one who thanks Hashem even for the beginning of service is brought further in.

If in the Sanzer Rav's time only the paroches was missing from the heavenly Beis Hamikdash, then today only small finishing touches remain, and a small generation completes the building with small deeds.
A sofer may not sit on a bench with the sefer Torah he himself wrote, which shows that the holiness came from Hashem through him as a messenger, not from him.
The angel who fought Yaakov withheld his name because an angel's name is his mission, and the yetzer hara's whole aim is that people should not know what they were sent for.
People travel precisely during the forty days of the meraglim because their travels are meant to repair the meraglim's flawed journey and turn Tisha B'Av into a festival.
A tree in the country may have waited more than five thousand years for a Jew to sit under it and learn Gemara, and fruits and streams wait for a particular soul to make a bracha on them.
Since Tammuz and Av are the two eyes, damaged by the meraglim's seeing, they bring the hardest tests of the eyes, and guarding the eyes then repairs that damage.

The Torah singles out the failings of only two nesi'im, Elitzur ben Shedeur in Korach's dispute and Shelumiel ben Tzurishaddai in the episode of Zimri, because their tribes correspond to Tammuz and Av.
A person may fall ill because he has finished his mission; changing his name gives him a new mission, and so a reason to go on living.
Adam, instead of blaming Chava for bringing death, called her 'mother of all life', looking at the good side; measure for measure Hashem then covered their shame with garments.
The world is like one huge computer: removing a single tiny screw ruins it, so even the smallest creature is indispensable.
The raven, which showed no mercy in the ark, abandons its own young, yet it fed Eliyahu, because Eliyahu is a soul of the days of Moshiach, when the raven will become merciful again.
The Megillah is a preview of the final redemption: when its time came everything happened in haste, because salvation comes from a place above time.
Hashem gives the cold according to the wool: the harshness of exile is measured to the warmth a person has to withstand it.
The 'depths' of the kapitel are the innermost point of the Jew, the place where he is a child of Hashem and where no sin ever reached; calling from there is what makes forgiveness possible.
The thirty-nine lashes instead of forty reflect that the highest of the levels of the soul is never touched by sin, so it is not struck.
The treasure of undeserved gifts flows from the Jew being Hashem's child: a father gives to a child not because he earned it but because a father must give.
Forgiveness leads to fear of Hashem in two ways: it keeps a sinner from despairing and abandoning himself, and it removes the barrier of sin so that he can feel Hashem's presence.
At a time destined for the geulah the Satan accuses that Jews are unworthy, and this is why such dates brought great troubles rather than redemption.
Not the irreligious, who are like children captured and know nothing, but machlokes and lashon hara among frum Jews spoiled the geulah.
The Mashgiach reads David's statement 'my heart was not haughty' as all the more striking because it comes from a king, the one person whose position would allow great aspirations.
Moshe, Avraham and David correspond to the three sources of influence on a person, his teacher, his father and his king, and each was a model of humility.
The splendor of tzaddikim of the house of David is no contradiction to their humility: it serves to arouse Heaven to restore the kingdom of David to its honor.
Envy of another's spiritual level comes from gaavah, so contentment with one's own portion is itself part of humility.
An infant can be given neither honor nor disgrace; this is the meaning of 'like a weaned child', the equanimity David describes.
David's restraint toward Shimi, though Shimi deserved death as a rebel, is what raised him to be the fourth leg of the Divine chariot, and it is also what made Purim possible through Mordechai.
Hashem 'remembers' David's suffering because the Satan sets itself against anyone who wants to do a great good, as it did to Avraham on the way to the Akeidah.

The Chashmonaim's cry 'Mi laHashem elai' was a repetition of Moshe's cry at the Golden Calf, when Shevet Levi set aside their own interests; the Chashmonaim, as Levi'im, renewed that mesiras nefesh, and the cry repeats every Chanukah.

Since nefesh means will, a person who bends his will for Hashem throughout the day performs mesiras nefesh in small pieces, which can outweigh a one-time giving of one's life, as in the mashal of the stone broken into pebbles.

Shevet Levi's lack of land is not a lack but a gift open to everyone: whoever looks to the Ribono shel Olam instead of a field as his inheritance joins Levi, and on Chanukah, the Yom Tov of the Chashmonaim who were Levi'im, every Jew can become part of that tribe.

In earlier times the Chanukah light was lit outside because the Jewish home was full of light and could shine into the street; today the street has entered the home, so the light must first be lit within.

Avraham's first test was mesiras nefesh for a G-d he had found by himself, before Hashem ever spoke to him; his last, the Akeidah, was a test of emunah against Hashem's own promise, and that last test is the pattern of the final test before Moshiach.

'Erev' means mixture, when things cannot be distinguished, while 'boker' comes from examining; the period before Moshiach is such an 'erev', and Chanukah's small light in the darkest season belongs to it.

The pesukim of the parshiyos read around Rosh Hashanah map the stages of teshuvah: Vayelech's 30 pesukim are the 30 days of the tzaddikim, and Haazinu's 52 are the 52 days until the final sealing on Shemini Atzeres.
The 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to Zos Chanukah equal the 122 pesukim of Nitzavim, Vayelech and Haazinu together, so that Chanukah contains the whole of the days of teshuvah.
Ki Savo, read to end the year with its curses, also has 122 pesukim, hinting that the curses of the passing year come from its 122 days of teshuvah left unused.

The 24 days from Rosh Chodesh Kislev to Chanukah correspond to the 24 letters of Baruch Shem, a lesser acceptance of the yoke of Heaven, and Chanukah to the 25 letters of Shema Yisrael, a greater one, just as Shema is printed in large letters and Baruch Shem in small ones.

Rosh Chodesh Kislev is the letter beis of Baruch, the true beginning of Chanukah, just as the Torah begins with the beis of Bereishis; as a first day that includes everything after it, this may be why it is called a day of teshuvah like Yom Kippur.
Zos Chanukah is hinted in the pasuk 'b'zos yechupar avon Yaakov', that through 'zos' the sin of Yaakov is atoned.
Since every mitzvah in the Torah has a continuation, the Mashgiach reads Chanukah, the last mitzvah from the last miracle, as pointing directly to the next miracle, the coming of Moshiach.

The Chanukah lamp below ten tefachim shows Hashem bending down to His children in galus, like a king who bends only for his own son; Chanukah is a weekday festival on which Hashem visits His sick people.

Tamar's delay was deliberate: because she carried Moshiach, she knew the Satan would block him, and only Yehuda's acceptance of public shame, a form of mesiras nefesh, could leave the Satan powerless.
Er and Onan fell not despite their lineage but because of it: the Satan concentrates all his force on the one from whom Moshiach is to come, as he would on the Kohen Gadol on Yom Kippur.
The unprecedented trials of this generation are themselves a sign of its role: the Satan knows this generation must bring Moshiach, so he throws at it tests no generation has had.
The Chanukah lamp stands opposite the mezuzah, which holds the Shema with its acceptance of mesiras nefesh, showing that the light of Moshiach is reached by giving up one's will for Hashem's.
What makes the Chanukah lights 'especially dear', unlike other mitzvos, is that Chanukah is the only festival created by human mesiras nefesh.
Since nefesh means will, mesiras nefesh is within everyone's reach daily: each time a Jew gives up his will, he gives over his nefesh.
Holding back a witty but hurtful remark, or not looking at what one should not see, is itself mesiras nefesh, the same quality that created Chanukah.
The answer to the Greek decree of 'no part in the G-d of Israel' is for each Jew to inscribe, as it were, on all his mitzvos that he has a part.
True self-sacrifice bends one's own comfort only; it never makes others pay for one's devotion, as Avraham Avinu showed.

The Mashgiach reads the extension of teshuvah until Zos Chanukah as a gift for weaker generations: the great generations were expected to finish by Yom Kippur, and the later, smaller ones were given more time.

The four stages of the season of teshuvah correspond to the number of pesukim in the parshiyos of that season, with Ki Savo's 122 pesukim equal to the 122 days from Rosh Chodesh Elul to the end of Chanukah.

Since Ki Savo belongs to the ending year with its curses, its 122 pesukim ask a person what he did with last year's 122 days, and the new 122 days call for a fresh start rather than the routine of past years.
Today the private domain of the Jewish home has become a public domain, connected through the media to every opinion in the world, and Chanukah's lights of Torah are the answer to this.

The nesiim read on Chanukah are, according to the Targum Yonasan as the Mashgiach brings it, a counter-weapon against the twelve princes of Yishmael, and the avodah of Chanukah can nullify their power.
Ner Chanukah, the last mitzvah, corresponds to the lowest Jew of the last generation, as the final letter of the Aseres Hadibros, the long final kaf of 'lerei'echa', reaches below the line.
Yaakov did not receive the name Yisrael when he defeated the angel, but only after the mesiras nefesh of Shechem, since the name means oneness with Hashem, and that is earned through mesiras nefesh.
When the sons of Yaakov said 'we will become one people', which Shechem had not even asked for, they were not speaking to Shechem but praying to Hashem for a wall between Israel and the nations.
Assimilation is like carrying out of the private domain into the public domain on Shabbos, and the Chanukah lamp at the doorway marks the techum of the Jewish domain.
The twenty-four days of Kislev before Chanukah correspond to the twenty-four letters of 'Baruch shem kevod', and the twenty-fifth to the twenty-five letters of Shema Yisrael.
The chassidim of Chabad who served Hashem with mesiras nefesh in Russia are today's Chashmonaim, and their merit brought about the fall of Soviet Russia.
The Mashgiach connects the summer travel season with the meraglim's forty days: the world travels in exactly these weeks because their failed journey must be repaired by journeys done right.
A seemingly trivial act, a brachah on a glass of water in a distant city, can be the very repair for which a person was sent there, and no one else can do it.
Noach did not spoil his portion of the world, so his animals remained righteous and his portion, Eretz Yisrael, was not flooded.
Following the Ba'al Shem Tov, Rashi and Onkelos do not argue about Bilaam: his blind eye, never defiled by looking at impurity, was the one that saw prophecy well.

The difference between the failed and successful spies was tefillah, and the two who had it are the ancestors of Moshiach ben Yosef and Moshiach ben Dovid, bringing redemption where the others brought exile.
Tzitzis means looking, and the mitzvah brings holiness into the eyes, the very organ with which the meraglim sinned.
All of creation sings to Hashem by doing His will, and a Jew's song is learning, davening and avoiding aveiros; one who does not is the lone exception in the choir.

The frog, at home both in water and on land, is the intermediate between the tahor and tamei kinds, so it embodies a mixture of good and evil; it therefore punished the Egyptians, whose plan to intermarry was an attempt to create exactly such a mixture.
Baruch shem is whispered because it proclaims that Hashem rules even in the places of the sitra achra; this is the frog's song, which is why it alone in Perek Shirah does not sing a passuk.

Ohalos and Negaim both open with 'shnayim' because tumah is division; Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah sent Rabbi Akiva there to show that the frog is neither purely 'one' nor purely 'two' but a mixture of both.
Rabbi Elazar ben Azaryah's words 'sharak lahem', she whistled to them, hint at the shuruk, the vowel of yesod, the attribute the frog corresponds to.

The sudden wave of modern inventions is a heavenly power of renewal sent down for the Jews; because they did not seize it, the nations and the sitra achra did, and it now takes away a Jew's peace and time.

Rabbi Elazar ben Arach, a soul with a spark of Moshiach, held on to 'hachodesh hazeh lachem', the first mitzvah, which belongs to the souls of Moshiach; his reading 'hacharesh haya libam' was a lament that the people's hearts did not hear the call of renewal.

The Mashgiach reads the terumas hadeshen, a night avodah that is only bedi'eved and done in work clothes, as the avodah most dear to Hashem, and sees in it the avodah of the generation before Moshiach and the sweeping of the house before Pesach.

The history of the world is told as four Nissans, each a narrower attempt at a perfected world: all of mankind, then only Klal Yisrael, then only the small corner of the Mishkan, and finally the geulah.

Moshe Rabbeinu's sin at Mei Merivah was a lack of emunah in himself: he saw himself as a policeman who strikes in Miriam's merit rather than a king whose word acts, and so Rav Hirsch pairs Shelach, Korach and Chukas with emunah in Hashem, in the chachamim, and in oneself.
The Targum's word for matzah, 'petir', means opening: Pesach is the opening, and the seder begins with opening a child's heart and ends with opening the door.
A person's strengths that come from his mazal are no cause for pride; his real test lies in the weakness of his animal, such as the lion's urge to tear at others or the snake's poison of speech.
Prayer itself is emunah: beyond asking for one's needs, the very act of turning to Hashem is pure faith.
In Nissan chesed pours from heaven like rain into a bucket; zerizus is the bucket that holds it, and laziness is the hole through which the blessing runs out.

There are four Nissans of Hashem's plan: creation, the Exodus and the Mishkan were each a smaller version of the original Gan Eden that was spoiled, and the fourth, the final redemption, is guaranteed to succeed.
The Mishkan was erected and dismantled seven times during the miluim and stood on the eighth, illustrating that a tzaddik falls seven times and rises.
Chametz is dough left standing out of laziness; it grows bigger only because air enters it, so its greatness is emptiness, whereas matzah is baked in haste and with kedushah.
Avraham Avinu is the spring of Yiddishkeit: as nature begins to grow in spring, Yiddishkeit began with the first Jew, whose month is Nissan.
The spring revival of nature after winter is itself tchiyas hameisim, which is why the haftarah of the dry bones is read on Pesach.

The Chasam Sofer's parable: the yetzer hara is a firm that, once people learn to beware of it, reopens under a new name, and its latest name is 'today's world', so the argument 'in today's world one does not do that' is the yetzer hara speaking.
Shlomis's 'shalom' is outward, reaching every passer-by, while Shulamis's 'shalom' is inner wholeness inside her own walls; Knesses Yisrael rejects the first and lives by the second.

The 'dance of the camps' that Knesses Yisrael asks of the nations is the separate camps of the desert, set against the camps of angels around the Kisei HaKavod, a society with no link to today's world.

The chutzpah and immorality of the Shoftim period in Megillas Ruth are the cover under which the root of Moshiach sprouted, hidden from the Satan, just as the signs of ikvesa d'meshicha at the end of Sotah open with chutzpah.
Yissachar's two hundred heads of Sanhedrin in the days of the return from Bavel, almost a thousand years later, show how long the influence of living next to Moshe and Aharon lasted.
Today's world is itself extreme, unashamed and breaking a tradition of generations, so the one who wants to stay normal must be what it calls 'extreme'.

The twelve paths in the sea against the seven streams of the future express the difference between a redemption still divided, like the twelve tribes, and the complete redemption of the seven, Shabbos and David.

The sea returned 'to its first condition' because its original condition was for the final redemption; it split early only for Yosef, whose self-sacrifice broke nature, and so it remains bound to that condition.
Yaakov's gift of 'zimras ha'aretz' was a niggun from Eretz Yisroel sent to awaken the union of Yosef and Yehuda, yesod and malchus, which led to 'Vayigash elav Yehuda'.
The piano's seven white keys of chesed and five black half-keys of din, together twelve, mirror exile, a song mixed with weeping; the future will have only the seven white tones.
Music whose tones have no connection to each other arouses lowly desires, because it is the opposite of the heavenly match that a true niggun is.
The war against the Jews in Eretz Yisroel is a war against Hashem, and it is decided in the batei medrash through Torah, tefillah and the daily Shirah.

Following the Tzemach Tzedek, the Mashgiach reads 'Hashem Elokeichem malkechem' not as a rejection of kingship but as its purpose: the people needed a king who would show them that Hashem is their King, a bridge through whose bittul they too become batel.
The Mashgiach explains that prostration on stone was allowed only in the Beis HaMikdash because full prostration expresses the greatest bittul, and that is possible only in the place of malchus.

Netilas yadayim, the Mashgiach explains, means lifting the hands: the ten fingers stand for all of a person's powers, and like Rebbi raising his ten fingers, one declares that nothing is for oneself, only for Hashem.

Shlomo's marriage to Pharaoh's daughter on the eve of the Mikdash's dedication was, for him, part of building it: he hoped to subdue the greatest kelipah and so spread malchus shamayim over the world, but that attempt failed and brought the decree of destruction.

The Mashgiach explains that the line of Moshiach always emerged through episodes that looked unseemly, so that the Satan would not suspect it, and only after Hashem's oath to David could it be revealed.
Since Shlomo was reincarnated in Yirmiyahu, the Mashgiach sees the season from Tisha b'Av to Shemini Atzeres as turning Yirmiyahu back into Shlomo, Eichah into Shir HaShirim, and churban into binyan.
Shemini Atzeres is not called 'chag', which means a circle, because it is the point in the center: Hashem Himself, without garments.
Middos are missing from the Torah not because they matter less, but because they are its entrance requirement: the Torah was given to people, and a person without middos is like an animal.
The barley Omer, animal food, brought on Pesach, and the human food brought on Shavuos mark the journey of Sefirah from beast to 'adam'.
Rachel's test, which brings the geulah, was not about how she davened or kept mitzvos but about her middos: she would not let her sister be shamed.
Tamar and Potiphar's wife both acted for Heaven's sake to bring Moshiach; the difference that made one praised and the other shamed forever was whether she was willing to shame another person.
The Divrei Chaim proves that burying a rasha is no mitzvah: though Jews buried the wicked during the plague of darkness, they still had no mitzvos and needed Pesach and milah.
The poor man's bird, burned with its foul-smelling feathers, is still a pleasing aroma to Hashem; so too a weak chiddush offered by a bochur must be received warmly.

'Panim' comes from 'penimiyus': each face shows a different neshamah and middos, so differing opinions each have a root, as Hillel's chessed and Shammai's gevurah showed on their faces and in their rulings.
What looked like rejection, the shrinking and then empty envelope, was in fact the Rebbe's way of bringing the disciple to the place where he had a task.
A single shehakol and borei nefashos said with kavanah at the edge of life brought a tikkun to souls that had waited for hundreds of years.
The mark of a talmid of Rebbe Reb Elimelech is that even when thirst makes a man like an animal, he stops to make a bracha with deveikus.
The particular tree, the particular water and the particular bread a person meets are each part of his shlichus, even when he thinks he is simply going his own way.

The Mashgiach reads the Hebrew servant's release at yovel as a picture of teshuvah: even one who has fallen so far that the seventh year cannot move him goes free when he hears the yovel shofar, as even the lost will come running at Moshiach's shofar.
Yovel is not just a law of land and servants but a law of creation: everything that wandered from its root must return, and teshuvah is that law applied to the soul hewn from the Kisei HaKavod.

The requirement that yovel apply only when all inhabitants are in the land is not a technical detail: yovel is the return to the root of Kol Yisrael where all souls are one, so without all Jews together there is no yovel, and likewise one who is not at peace with other Jews is not in the world of Yom Kippur.
The Mashgiach explains why the tekiah blown after Yom Kippur has no teruah: it is already an awakening of the shofar gadol of Moshiach, the climax of return.

Melaveh malkah belongs to David HaMelech, the greatest, precisely because it comes after Shabbos: at the end of each seven there is a chance that instead of a new week the eighth day of Moshiach, a day that is all Shabbos, will begin.

The Mashgiach calls the Tishrei after shemittah the 'shalosh seudos' of shemittah: just as the end of Shabbos is a time of eis ratzon, the end of the shemittah year is a great eis ratzon when prayers are accepted.
The mezuzah and the ner Chanukah face opposite directions: the mezuzah, on the right of one entering, guards the inside; the ner Chanukah, on the right of one leaving, sends the kedushah outward.
The same pairing runs through milah and priah, and through lo sa'aseh and mitzvas aseh: one keeps the outside forces away, the other reveals the glory of Hashem.
The cold of a mitzvah done without feeling is purified by snow, and the eight lights of Zos Chanukah are the fire that stands against that snow.
Because the eighth day is above time, it is not confined to its days and can stretch the light of Chanukah over the whole year.
The Beraisa fixes Chanukah through Hallel and hoda'ah rather than the lights because these are what remain after the lighting ends.
Since Hallel on Chanukah is a full obligation, it gives its kedushah to the whole of Shacharis, as a day with Mussaf gives Shacharis the kedushah of Mussaf.
